claim: Candida albicans is one of the most common human fungal pathogens.
source: Candida albicans is one of the most common human fungal pathogens.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about C. albicans prevalence in human fungal infections.

claim: C. albicans pathogenesis is tightly linked to its ability to undergo a morphogenetic transition from typically budding yeast to filamentous forms of hyphae and pseudohyphae.
source: C. albicans pathogenesis is tightly linked to its ability to under a morphogenetic transition from typically budding yeast to filamentous forms of hyphae and pseudohyphae.
evidence: This statement draws on established scientific consensus about the relationship between morphogenesis and pathogenesis in C. albicans.

claim: Nearly all studies of C. albicans filamentous morphogenesis have been based on in vitro induction of filamentation.
source: Filamentous morphogenesis is the most intensively studied C. albicans virulence traits; however, nearly all of these studies have been based on in vitro induction of filamentation.
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature on C. albicans morphogenesis research.

claim: Three core positive regulators of filament initiation in vivo are Efg1, Brg1, and Rob1.
source: Three core positive (Efg1, Brg1, and Rob1) and two core negative regulators (Nrg1 and Tup1) of filament initiation were identified.
evidence: This claim is supported by the genetic screen data presented in the manuscript showing these mutants formed fewer than 30% filamentous cells.

claim: Two core negative regulators of filament initiation in vivo are Nrg1 and Tup1.
source: Three core positive (Efg1, Brg1, and Rob1) and two core negative regulators (Nrg1 and Tup1) of filament initiation were identified.
evidence: This claim is supported by the genetic screen data showing these deletion mutants had increased filamentation.

claim: No previous systematic analysis of genes affecting the elongation step of filamentation has been reported.
source: No previous systematic analysis of genes affecting the elongation step has been reported and we found that large set of transcription factors affect filament elongation in vivo including four (Hms1, Lys14, War1, Dal81) with no effect on in vitro elongation.
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature indicating a gap in knowledge.

claim: Four transcription factors (Hms1, Lys14, War1, Dal81) affect filament elongation in vivo but have no effect on in vitro elongation.
source: No previous systematic analysis of genes affecting the elongation step has been reported and we found that large set of transcription factors affect filament elongation in vivo including four (Hms1, Lys14, War1, Dal81) with no effect on in vitro elongation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing in vivo and in vitro filament elongation phenotypes.

claim: The gene targets of initiation and elongation regulators are distinct.
source: We also show that the gene targets of initiation and elongation regulators are distinct.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data comparing regulators of initiation versus elongation.

claim: Efg1 primarily functions to mediate relief of Nrg1 repression.
source: Genetic interaction analysis of the core positive and negative regulators revealed that the master regulator Efg1 primarily functions to mediate relief of Nrg1 repression and is dispensable for expression of hypha-associated genes in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic interaction experiments showing that deletion of NRG1 suppresses the efg1 deletion phenotype.

claim: Efg1 is dispensable for expression of hypha-associated genes in vitro and in vivo after relief of Nrg1 repression.
source: Genetic interaction analysis of the core positive and negative regulators revealed that the master regulator Efg1 primarily functions to mediate relief of Nrg1 repression and is dispensable for expression of hypha-associated genes in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data showing that hypha-associated genes are expressed at WT levels in the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ double mutant.

claim: The ability to transition between round, budding yeast and filamentous hyphae and pseudohyphae is positively correlated with C. albicans ability to cause both mucosal and invasive infections.
source: In Candida albicans, one of the most common human fungal pathogens, the ability to transition between round, budding yeast and filamentous hyphae and pseudohyphae is positively correlated with its ability to cause both mucosal and invasive infections (Lopes and Lionakis, 2022; Sudbery, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Establishment of the commensal state of C. albicans within the gastrointestinal tract is negatively correlated with filamentation.
source: Conversely, establishment of the commensal state of C. albicans within the gastrointestinal tract is negatively correlated with filamentation (Witchley et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The yeast form is thought to be required for dissemination within the blood stream.
source: Furthermore, the yeast form is thought to be required for dissemination within the blood stream while transition to hyphae contributes to tissue damage in both disseminated and mucosal disease (Saville et al., 2003; Meir et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Transition to hyphae contributes to tissue damage in both disseminated and mucosal disease.
source: Furthermore, the yeast form is thought to be required for dissemination within the blood stream while transition to hyphae contributes to tissue damage in both disseminated and mucosal disease (Saville et al., 2003; Meir et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The extensive literature on C. albicans morphogenesis has been almost entirely focused on the in vitro induction of the yeast-to-hyphae transition.
source: To date, the extensive literature devoted to understanding the mechanisms of C. albicans morphogenesis has been almost entirely focused on the in vitro induction of the yeast-to-hyphae transition (Sudbery, 2011; Villa et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature supported by citations.

claim: It is not clear how many genes and pathways involved in in vitro filamentation are also involved in C. albicans filamentation in vivo.
source: A significant knowledge gap is that it is not clear how many of these genes and pathways are also involved in C. albicans filamentation in vivo.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current scientific knowledge.

claim: The cAMP-protein kinase A pathway is required for initiation of filamentation in almost all in vitro conditions.
source: For example, the cAMP-protein kinase A pathway is required for initiation of filamentation in almost all in vitro conditions; specifically, strains lacking the adenylyl cyclase gene (CYR1) or the PKA catalytic subunits (TPK1/2) remain in yeast phase under hyphae-inducing conditions (Cao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Strains lacking the adenylyl cyclase gene (CYR1) or the PKA catalytic subunits (TPK1/2) remain in yeast phase under hyphae-inducing conditions in vitro.
source: For example, the cAMP-protein kinase A pathway is required for initiation of filamentation in almost all in vitro conditions; specifically, strains lacking the adenylyl cyclase gene (CYR1) or the PKA catalytic subunits (TPK1/2) remain in yeast phase under hyphae-inducing conditions (Cao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: cyr1∆∆ and tpk1∆∆ tpk2∆∆ mutants form hyphae in vivo to nearly the same extent as WT cells.
source: In contrast, cyr1∆∆ and tpk1∆∆ tpk2∆∆ mutants form hyphae in vivo to nearly the same extent as WT cells, indicating that this pathway plays a minor role in the regulating the switch between morphotypes in vivo (Wakade et al., 2022a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The PKA pathway plays a minor role in regulating the switch between morphotypes in vivo.
source: In contrast, cyr1∆∆ and tpk1∆∆ tpk2∆∆ mutants form hyphae in vivo to nearly the same extent as WT cells, indicating that this pathway plays a minor role in the regulating the switch between morphotypes in vivo (Wakade et al., 2022a).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data cited.

claim: The length of the filaments formed by cyr1∆∆ and tpk1∆∆ tpk2∆∆ mutants is shorter than WT.
source: The length of the filaments formed by these mutants is shorter than WT (Wakade et al., 2022b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The PKA pathway switches from controlling initiation of hyphae formation in vitro to regulating maintenance of hyphal extension in vivo.
source: Consequently, the PKA pathway appears to switch from controlling initiation of hyphae formation in vitro to regulating maintenance of hyphal extension in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of in vitro and in vivo phenotypes of PKA pathway mutants.

claim: A total of 155 transcription factor deletion mutants were screened for effects on in vivo filamentation.
source: To further characterize the regulation of C. albicans filamentation in vivo, we screened a collection of 155 transcription factor (TF) deletion mutants (Homann et al., 2009) for those with either reduced hyphae/yeast ratios or filament length.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: At least 40 transcription factor mutants from the Homann collection had effects on morphogenesis in vitro.
source: As part of their characterization of a collection of 155 TF deletion mutants, Homann et al. reported that at least 40 mutants had effects, both positive and negative, on morphogenesis in vitro (Homann et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: All TF mutants, with the exception of the efg1∆∆ mutant, formed some proportion of filamentous cells in vivo.
source: We found that all TF mutants, with the exception of the efg1∆∆ mutant, formed some proportion of filamentous cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results from the genetic screen.

claim: A total of 19 TF mutants showed a statistically significant reduction (p<0.05) in the percentage of filaments relative to the reference strain.
source: A total of 19 TF mutants showed a statistically significant reduction (p<0.05, paired Student's t test) in the percentage of filaments relative the reference strain (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Only two mutants (tup1∆∆ and nrg1∆∆) showed statistically significant increases in the proportion of filaments.
source: Only two mutants (tup1∆∆ and nrg1∆∆) showed statistically significant increases in the proportion of filaments; Tup1 and Nrg1 are well-characterized repressors of filamentation in vitro (Sudbery, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to previous literature characterizing these genes.

claim: Tup1 and Nrg1 are well-characterized repressors of filamentation in vitro.
source: Only two mutants (tup1∆∆ and nrg1∆∆) showed statistically significant increases in the proportion of filaments; Tup1 and Nrg1 are well-characterized repressors of filamentation in vitro (Sudbery, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Core regulators of in vivo filamentation are defined as mutants that formed fewer than 30% filamentous cells.
source: We classified the TF mutants with reduced filamentation into two groups: (1) core regulators of in vivo filamentation (EFG1, BRG1, ROB1), defined as mutants that formed fewer than 30% filamentous cells, and (2) auxiliary regulators, defined as mutants with a statistically significant change in filamentation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a definition established by the authors for classifying their experimental results.

claim: Auxiliary regulators are defined as mutants with a statistically significant change in filamentation.
source: We classified the TF mutants with reduced filamentation into two groups: (1) core regulators of in vivo filamentation (EFG1, BRG1, ROB1), defined as mutants that formed fewer than 30% filamentous cells, and (2) auxiliary regulators, defined as mutants with a statistically significant change in filamentation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a definition established by the authors for classifying their experimental results.

claim: The efg1∆∆ mutant formed essentially no filaments in vivo.
source: The efg1∆∆ mutant formed essentially no filaments in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Deletion of BRG1, ROB1, TEC1, and RIM101 reduced the ratio of filaments/yeast but each of these homozygous deletion mutants formed filaments.
source: Deletion of BRG1, ROB1, TEC1, and RIM101 reduced the ratio of filaments/yeast but each of these homozygous deletion mutants formed filaments.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Similar results were observed with efg1∆∆, brg1∆∆, rob1∆∆, tec1∆∆, and rim101∆∆ mutants in vitro using RPMI+10% FBS medium at 37°C as inducing conditions.
source: Similar results were observed with these five mutants in vitro using RPMI+10% FBS medium at 37°C as inducing conditions (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Five TF deletion mutants (TEC1, RIM101, CPH2, AHR1, ISW2, NDT80, SFL2) were reported to be deficient for filamentation in vitro.
source: Among the auxiliary regulators, a total of five TF deletion mutants were reported in the literature (Homann et al., 2009) to be deficient for filamentation in vitro (TEC1, RIM101, CPH2, AHR1, ISW2, NDT80, SFL2) while three mutants showed the opposite phenotype of increased filamentation in vitro but decreased filamentation in vivo (FGR15, ZCF3, 19.6874).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Three mutants (FGR15, ZCF3, 19.6874) showed increased filamentation in vitro but decreased filamentation in vivo.
source: Among the auxiliary regulators, a total of five TF deletion mutants were reported in the literature (Homann et al., 2009) to be deficient for filamentation in vitro (TEC1, RIM101, CPH2, AHR1, ISW2, NDT80, SFL2) while three mutants showed the opposite phenotype of increased filamentation in vitro but decreased filamentation in vivo (FGR15, ZCF3, 19.6874).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of literature data with the current experimental results.

claim: Five TF deletion mutants (GRF10, SEF1, ZCF31, 19.1150, 19.2730) had reduced filamentation in vivo but no reported effect on filamentation in vitro.
source: Finally, five TF deletion mutants had reduced filamentation in vivo but no reported effect on filamentation in vitro (GRF10, SEF1, ZCF31, 19.1150, 19.2730).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of current experimental data with literature reports.

claim: The stp2∆∆ mutant showed reduced filamentation in vivo.
source: The stp2∆∆ mutant showed reduced filamentation as well; however, Stp2 regulates amino acid uptake (Miramón and Lorenz, 2016) and we suspected this phenotype may represent a genetic interaction with the arg4∆∆ mutation present in this background (Noble and Johnson, 2005); consistent with this hypothesis, re-introduction of the ARG4 gene to the stp2∆∆ mutant restored normal filamentation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Stp2 regulates amino acid uptake.
source: The stp2∆∆ mutant showed reduced filamentation as well; however, Stp2 regulates amino acid uptake (Miramón and Lorenz, 2016) and we suspected this phenotype may represent a genetic interaction with the arg4∆∆ mutation present in this background (Noble and Johnson, 2005); consistent with this hypothesis, re-introduction of the ARG4 gene to the stp2∆∆ mutant restored normal filamentation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Re-introduction of the ARG4 gene to the stp2∆∆ mutant restored normal filamentation.
source: The stp2∆∆ mutant showed reduced filamentation as well; however, Stp2 regulates amino acid uptake (Miramón and Lorenz, 2016) and we suspected this phenotype may represent a genetic interaction with the arg4∆∆ mutation present in this background (Noble and Johnson, 2005); consistent with this hypothesis, re-introduction of the ARG4 gene to the stp2∆∆ mutant restored normal filamentation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Efg1 has been a well-studied master regulator of in vitro filamentation.
source: Efg1 has been a well-studied master regulator of in vitro filamentation (Glazier, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Deletion of EFG1 in a set of four well-characterized clinical strains consistently eliminated filamentation in vivo.
source: We had previously shown that deletion of EFG1 in a set of four well-characterized clinical strains with varying levels of in vivo filamentation consistently eliminated filamentation (Wakade et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The P94015 clinical isolate contains a natural EFG1 loss-of-function mutation.
source: Among these strains, Hirakawa found one that contained a natural EFG1 loss-of-function mutation (P94015).
evidence: This claim is based on previous characterization of clinical isolates.

claim: The P94015 strain was essentially afilamentous in vivo.
source: Consistent with its inability to filament in vitro and its lack of a functional copy of EFG1, the P94015 strain was essentially afilamentous in vivo (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Efg1 is an important regulator of filamentation within infected tissue.
source: These data indicate that Efg1 is an important regulator of filamentation within infected tissue.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing that strains lacking functional Efg1 do not filament in vivo.

claim: A total of 59 TF deletion mutants had a statistically significant reduction in filament length (p<0.05) relative to WT strains.
source: A total of 59 TF deletion mutants had a statistically significant reduction in filament length (paired Student's t test, p<0.05) relative to WT strains (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Only two mutants, nrg1∆∆ and tup1∆∆, showed increased filament length.
source: Only two mutants, nrg1∆∆ and tup1∆∆, showed increased filament length.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: 31 TF mutants formed filaments that were 25% shorter than WT.
source: Of the set of mutants with reduced filament length, 31 formed filaments that were 25% shorter than WT (Figure 2B); representative distributions of filament lengths for two of these mutants (hms1∆∆ and lys14∆∆) are shown in Figure 2C.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: There has been no systematic or large-scale genetic screen for mutants with reduced filament length.
source: To our knowledge, there has been no systematic or large-scale genetic screen for mutants with reduced filament length.
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature indicating a gap in knowledge.

claim: Five TF deletion mutants (HMS1, LYS14, SEF1, DAL81, and WAR1) have strong defects in filament length but no known in vitro filamentation phenotypes.
source: We, therefore, selected five TF deletion mutants (HMS1, LYS14, SEF1, DAL81, and WAR1) with strong defects in filament length but no known in vitro filamentation phenotypes.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of current experimental data with literature reports.

claim: The five mutants (hms1∆∆, lys14∆∆, sef1∆∆, dal81∆∆, and war1∆∆) formed filaments in vitro with lengths that were not significantly different than WT.
source: The five mutants formed filaments in vitro with lengths that were not significantly different than WT (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Ume6 is a TF that is required for hyphal elongation in vitro.
source: Ume6 is a TF that is required for hyphal elongation in vitro (Banerjee et al., 2008) but its deletion mutant is not included in the Homann collection (Homann et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The ume6∆∆ mutant forms filaments to the same extent of WT in vivo.
source: In vivo, the ume6∆∆ mutant forms filaments to the same extent of WT but, consistent with its in vitro phenotype, the filaments are 40% shorter (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The ume6∆∆ mutant forms filaments that are 40% shorter than WT in vivo.
source: In vivo, the ume6∆∆ mutant forms filaments to the same extent of WT but, consistent with its in vitro phenotype, the filaments are 40% shorter (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Deletion of UME6 in clinical isolates has a minimal effect on filament initiation.
source: We had previously shown that deletion of UME6 in clinical isolates has a minimal effect on filament initiation but we did not assess its role in elongation in that study (Wakade et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Deletion of UME6 consistently leads to shorter filaments in three clinical isolates that form filaments.
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, re-analysis of those data revealed that deletion of UME6 consistently leads to shorter filaments in the three clinical isolates that form filaments.
evidence: This claim is supported by re-analysis of previous data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ume6 functions mainly to regulate genes involved in hyphal elongation or maintenance rather than filament initiation in vivo.
source: This indicates that Ume6 functions mainly to regulate genes involved in hyphal elongation or maintenance rather than filament initiation in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing Ume6 affects elongation but not initiation.

claim: The screen identified a total of 37 mutants that affected either initiation of filament formation (8 mutants), filament elongation (16 mutants), or both (15 mutants).
source: As summarized in Figure 2F, our screen identified at total of 37 mutants that affected either initiation of filament formation (8 mutants), filament elongation (16 mutants), or both (15 mutants).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Of the TFs that only affect initiation, 5 have in vitro phenotypes that match their in vivo phenotype.
source: Of the TFs that only affect initiation, 5 have in vitro phenotypes that match their in vivo phenotype; the 19.8874∆∆ mutant shows increased filamentation in vitro while neither 19.2730 nor 19.1150 have been reported to affect filamentation.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of current experimental data with literature reports.

claim: Of the TFs that only affect elongation, HMS1, UME6, and ZCF29 (3/14) have been shown to have phenotypes in vitro.
source: Of the TFs that only affect elongation, HMS1, UME6, and ZCF29 (3/14) have been shown to have phenotypes in vitro.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of current experimental data with literature reports.

claim: Most of the elongation-associated TFs have not been found to have filamentation defects using standard in vitro assays.
source: Thus, most of the elongation-associated TFs have not been found to have filamentation defects using standard in vitro assays.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of in vitro and in vivo phenotypes.

claim: Filament length has not been systematically studied prior to this work.
source: It is important to keep in mind that filament length has not been systematically studied prior to this work and, to our knowledge, no large-scale genetic characterization of genes affecting elongation has been reported.
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature indicating a gap in knowledge.

claim: Lys14, Hms1, and Ume6 are required for virulence in disseminated candidiasis.
source: Lys14, Hms1, and Ume6, specific regulators of elongation in vivo, are required for virulence in disseminated candidiasis (Banerjee et al., 2008; Pérez et al., 2013), suggesting that this phenotype is relevant to pathogenesis, particularly since LYS14 and HMS1 mutants have few other in vitro phenotypes (Homann et al., 2009; Shapiro et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: LYS14 and HMS1 mutants have few other in vitro phenotypes.
source: Lys14, Hms1, and Ume6, specific regulators of elongation in vivo, are required for virulence in disseminated candidiasis (Banerjee et al., 2008; Pérez et al., 2013), suggesting that this phenotype is relevant to pathogenesis, particularly since LYS14 and HMS1 mutants have few other in vitro phenotypes (Homann et al., 2009; Shapiro et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The brg1∆∆, efg1∆∆, and rob1∆∆ mutants altered the expression of environmentally responsive genes under both in vitro and in vivo conditions.
source: Consistent with their roles in both in vivo and in vitro filamentation, the brg1∆∆, efg1∆∆, and rob1∆∆ mutants altered the expression of the environmentally responsive genes under both in vitro and in vivo conditions (Figure 3A, B, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data shown in Figure 3A, B and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Efg1 is the dominant TF in vitro based on the number of genes it regulates.
source: From the chord plots, Efg1 is the dominant TF in vitro while Rob1 regulates a larger number of this set of genes in vivo.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the chord plots shown in Figure 3.

claim: Rob1 regulates a larger number of environmentally responsive genes in vivo compared to Efg1.
source: From the chord plots, Efg1 is the dominant TF in vitro while Rob1 regulates a larger number of this set of genes in vivo.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the chord plots shown in Figure 3.

claim: Brg1 regulates a similarly sized set of genes under both in vitro and in vivo conditions.
source: In contrast, Brg1 regulates a similarly sized set of genes under both conditions.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of transcriptional profiling data in vitro and in vivo.

claim: There is overlap between the in vitro and in vivo sets of genes regulated by each TF, but there are more genes that are regulated only in vitro or in vivo.
source: Although there is overlap between the in vitro and in vivo sets of genes regulated by each TF, there are more genes that are regulated only in vitro or in vivo (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The direct and/or indirect target set of each TF is dependent on the environment.
source: These data suggest that the direct and/or indirect target set of each TF is dependent on the environment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that different genes are regulated in vitro versus in vivo.

claim: 67% of genes downregulated in the efg1∆∆ mutant in vivo were also downregulated in one of the other two core mutants (brg1∆∆ or rob1∆∆).
source: Focusing on the in vivo expression data, a significant percentage of genes downregulated in the efg1∆∆ mutant (67%) was also downregulated in one of the other two mutants (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 72% of genes downregulated in the rob1∆∆ mutant in vivo were also downregulated in one of the other two core mutants.
source: For the rob1∆∆ mutant, the percentage of overlap was similar to the efg1∆∆ mutant (72%) while all but five genes (83%) downregulated in the brg1∆∆ mutant were downregulated in at least one of the other two mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Venn diagram analysis.

claim: 83% of genes downregulated in the brg1∆∆ mutant in vivo were also downregulated in at least one of the other two core mutants.
source: For the rob1∆∆ mutant, the percentage of overlap was similar to the efg1∆∆ mutant (72%) while all but five genes (83%) downregulated in the brg1∆∆ mutant were downregulated in at least one of the other two mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Venn diagram analysis.

claim: A similar pattern of overlap is evident for upregulated genes: efg1∆∆ (62%); rob1∆∆ (77%); and brg1∆∆ (79%).
source: A similar pattern of overlap is also evident for upregulated genes: efg1∆∆ (62%); rob1∆∆ (77%); and brg1∆∆ (79%).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the transcriptional profiling data.

claim: The key regulators of filament initiation have overlapping effects on the expression of environmentally responsive genes in vivo and in vitro.
source: Thus, the key regulators of filament initiation have overlapping effects on the expression of environmentally responsive genes in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the overlap analysis of gene expression data.

claim: Brg1, Efg1, and Rob1 regulate the expression of other TFs required for the normal transition from yeast-to-filaments.
source: Brg1, Efg1, and Rob1 regulate the expression of other TFs required for the normal transition from yeast-to-filaments.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data showing effects on other TF genes.

claim: In vitro, Efg1 affects the expression of six other regulators including both negative regulators.
source: In vitro, Efg1 affects the expression of six other regulators including both negative regulators (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Neither Rob1 nor Brg1 affect the expression of any other positive regulator of TF in the probe set in vitro but negatively regulate Nrg1.
source: Neither Rob1 nor Brg1 affect the expression of any other positive regulator of TF in our probe set but negatively regulate Nrg1.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data.

claim: Only Efg1 affects the expression of TUP1.
source: Only Efg1 affects the expression of TUP1.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data.

claim: The regulatory relationships between Brg1, Efg1, and Rob1 remain the same in vivo as in vitro.
source: The regulatory relationships between Brg1, Efg1, and Rob1 remain the same in vivo (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of transcriptional profiling data in vitro and in vivo shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Brg1 is the only factor that negatively regulates Nrg1 in vivo.
source: Interestingly, Brg1 is the only factor that negative regulates Nrg1, although Efg1 plays a role indirectly through its activation of Brg1.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data in vivo.

claim: Efg1 plays a role in negatively regulating Nrg1 indirectly through its activation of Brg1.
source: Interestingly, Brg1 is the only factor that negative regulates Nrg1, although Efg1 plays a role indirectly through its activation of Brg1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the transcriptional profiling data showing Efg1 activates Brg1 and Brg1 represses Nrg1.

claim: In vivo, Brg1, Efg1, and Rob1 each positively regulate two other positive regulators.
source: In vivo, Brg1, Efg1, and Rob1 each positively regulate two other positive regulators, leading to a much more interconnected set of network interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data in vivo.

claim: Efg1-Brg1-Tec1 and Efg1-Brg1-Ahr1 both appear to form feedforward loops.
source: Efg1-Brg1-Tec1 and Efg1-Brg1-Ahr1 both appear to form feedforward loops.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the transcriptional profiling data showing regulatory relationships.

claim: The network structure of the TFs affecting in vivo filament initiation is distinct from that present during in vitro filamentation.
source: Thus, the network structure of the TFs affecting in vivo filament initiation is distinct from that present during in vitro filamentation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparison of the regulatory networks in vitro and in vivo.

claim: EFG1, BRG1, ROB1, and TEC1 interact functionally during in vitro filament formation.
source: We previously found that these four genes interact functionally during in vitro filament formation as measured by the proportion of filaments formed (Figure 5A, Glazier et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work and data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In vivo, EFG1 and BRG1 interacted with TEC1.
source: In vivo, EFG1 and BRG1 interacted with TEC1 (Figure 5B, C) while no other combinations showed a statistically significant change in the proportion of filaments formed.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: No other combinations of heterozygous deletions in EFG1, BRG1, ROB1, and TEC1 showed a statistically significant change in the proportion of filaments formed in vivo.
source: In vivo, EFG1 and BRG1 interacted with TEC1 (Figure 5B, C) while no other combinations showed a statistically significant change in the proportion of filaments formed.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic interaction data.

claim: The network of functional interactions between these regulators in vivo is distinct from that observed in vitro.
source: Thus, the network of functional interactions between these regulators in vivo is distinct from that observed in vitro.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparison of genetic interaction data in vitro and in vivo.

claim: The functional genetic interactions between Efg1, Brg1, and Tec1 is consistent with the feedforward loop indicated by in vivo transcriptional data.
source: The functional genetic interactions between Efg1, Brg1, and Tec1 is consistent with the feedforward loop indicated by our in vivo transcriptional data (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an inference connecting genetic interaction data with transcriptional profiling data.

claim: Neither the efg1∆ mutant nor the tec1∆ mutant showed altered filamentation in vivo.
source: Although neither the efg1∆ mutant nor the tec1∆ mutant showed altered filamentation in vivo, both mutants affected gene expression with 43 (efg1∆) and 52 (tec1∆) genes differentially expressed (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Both efg1∆ and tec1∆ mutants affected gene expression with 43 (efg1∆) and 52 (tec1∆) genes differentially expressed in vivo.
source: Although neither the efg1∆ mutant nor the tec1∆ mutant showed altered filamentation in vivo, both mutants affected gene expression with 43 (efg1∆) and 52 (tec1∆) genes differentially expressed (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data.

claim: There is substantial overlap in the sets of genes regulated by the efg1∆, tec1∆ single mutants and the efg1∆ tec1∆ double mutant.
source: As shown in the network diagram in Figure 5D, there is substantial overlap in the sets of genes regulated by the single mutants and the double mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by the network diagram shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The sets of genes downregulated in the single heterozygous mutants of efg1∆ and tec1∆ showed 72% and 60% overlap, respectively.
source: The sets of genes downregulated in the single heterozygous mutants of efg1∆ and tec1∆ were very similar with 72% and 60% overlap, respectively (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of transcriptional profiling data.

claim: The double heterozygous efg1∆ tec1∆ mutant showed 83% overlap with the two single heterozygotes.
source: Furthermore, the double heterozygous efg1∆ tec1∆ mutant also showed significant overlap with the two single heterozygotes (83%), indicating that Tec1 and Efg1 regulate similar sets of genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of transcriptional profiling data.

claim: Tec1 and Efg1 regulate similar sets of genes.
source: Furthermore, the double heterozygous efg1∆ tec1∆ mutant also showed significant overlap with the two single heterozygotes (83%), indicating that Tec1 and Efg1 regulate similar sets of genes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the overlap analysis of gene expression data.

claim: The set of genes regulated by Efg1 and Tec1 contains TFs that affect in vivo filamentation as well as hypha-specific genes.
source: The set of genes regulated by Efg1 and Tec1 contains TFs that affect in vivo filamentation as well as hypha-specific genes (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of transcriptional profiling data.

claim: Efg1 and Tec1 showed a negative genetic interaction with respect to the expression of 7 out of 10 TFs involved in in vivo filamentation.
source: As shown in Figure 6B, Efg1 and Tec1 showed a negative genetic interaction with respect to the expression of 7 out of 10 TFs involved in in vivo filamentation.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic interaction analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A negative genetic interaction suggests that Efg1 and Tec1 are local hubs that interdependently regulate other filamentation-associated TFs in vivo.
source: This negative interaction suggests that Efg1 and Tec1 are local hubs that interdependently regulate other filamentation-associated TFs in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic interaction analysis.

claim: Efg1 and Tec1 regulate hypha-specific genes independently because no ε values were outside of the ±0.2 range.
source: In contrast, Efg1 and Tec1 regulate hypha-specific genes independently because no ε values were outside of the ±0.2 range (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic interaction analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The cooperative interactions between Efg1 and Tec1 are not observed in vitro.
source: Interestingly, the cooperative interactions between Efg1 and Tec1 are not observed in vitro (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of genetic interaction data in vitro and in vivo.

claim: The functional genetic interaction between Efg1 and Tec1 is due to their cooperative role in the regulation of other TFs that affect filamentation.
source: Our data support the conclusion that the functional genetic interaction between Efg1 and Tec1 is due to their cooperative role in the regulation of other TFs that affect filamentation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic interaction and transcriptional profiling data.

claim: Of the TFs whose deletion mutants affected filament length, 15 have no effect on the yeast-to-filament transition.
source: Of the TFs whose deletion mutants affected filament length, 15 have no effect on the yeast-to-filament transition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the genetic screen.

claim: Ume6 regulates hyphal maintenance under in vitro conditions and has been considered one of the master regulators of hyphae formation.
source: Ume6 regulates hyphal maintenance under in vitro conditions and has been considered one of the master regulators of hyphae formation.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about Ume6.

claim: Loss of UME6 has a significant effect on the length of filaments formed in vivo but no effect on the yeast-to-filament transition.
source: Consistent with the pioneering work of the Kadosh laboratory (Banerjee et al., 2008), loss of UME6 has a significant effect on the length of filaments formed in vivo but no effect on the yeast-to-filament transition (Figure 2E/F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E/F and a citation to previous literature.

claim: HMS1 is a TF previously found to affect filamentation at high temperature (42°C) in vitro.
source: We also selected two additional TFs whose mutants have reduced filament length but no change in filament initiation to study: HMS1, a TF previously found to affect filamentation at high temperature (42°C, Shapiro et al., 2012) in vitro, and LYS14, a TF with no morphology or other in vitro phenotype (Homann et al., 2009; Pérez et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: LYS14 is a TF with no morphology or other in vitro phenotype.
source: We also selected two additional TFs whose mutants have reduced filament length but no change in filament initiation to study: HMS1, a TF previously found to affect filamentation at high temperature (42°C, Shapiro et al., 2012) in vitro, and LYS14, a TF with no morphology or other in vitro phenotype (Homann et al., 2009; Pérez et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: LYS14 is homologous to Saccharomyces cerevisiae TFs involved in the regulation of lysine biosynthesis genes, but this function is not conserved in C. albicans.
source: Although LYS14 is homologous to Saccharomyces cerevisiae TFs involved in the regulation of lysine biosynthesis genes, this function is not conserved in C. albicans and little else is known about its role in C. albicans biology (Pérez et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Deletion mutants of HMS1 and LYS14 have reduced competitive fitness in a mouse model of disseminated candidiasis.
source: Deletion mutants of HMS1 and LYS14 have reduced competitive fitness in a mouse model of disseminated candidiasis while the hms1∆∆ mutant is also less fit during GI colonization (Pérez et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The hms1∆∆ mutant is less fit during GI colonization.
source: Deletion mutants of HMS1 and LYS14 have reduced competitive fitness in a mouse model of disseminated candidiasis while the hms1∆∆ mutant is also less fit during GI colonization (Pérez et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Strains lacking UME6 have reduced virulence in the disseminated infection model.
source: Strains lacking UME6 have reduced virulence in the disseminated infection model but are hyper-fit during GI colonization (Witchley et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Strains lacking UME6 are hyper-fit during GI colonization.
source: Strains lacking UME6 have reduced virulence in the disseminated infection model but are hyper-fit during GI colonization (Witchley et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Neither Ume6, Lys14, nor Hms1 have a consistent effect on the expression of most hyphae-associated genes in vivo.
source: Neither Ume6, Lys14, nor Hms1 have a consistent effect on the expression of most hyphae-associated genes in vivo (Figure 7A, Supplementary file 5), particularly when compared with the core regulators of filament initiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data shown in Figure 7A and Supplementary file 5.

claim: HYR1 and HWP1 are the only genes downregulated by >2-fold in the deletion mutants of all three elongation-associated TFs (Ume6, Lys14, Hms1).
source: Of the hyphae-associated genes, HYR1 and HWP1 are the only gene downregulated by >2-fold in the deletion mutants of all three elongation-associated TFs.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data.

claim: Ume6 plays the most prominent role in the expression of hyphae-associated genes among the three elongation-associated TFs.
source: Of the three TFs involved in hyphal elongation, Ume6 plays the most prominent role in the expression of hyphae-associated genes (Figure 7A) and affects the expression of 6/9 genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Ume6 affects the expression of 6/9 hyphae-associated genes.
source: Of the three TFs involved in hyphal elongation, Ume6 plays the most prominent role in the expression of hyphae-associated genes (Figure 7A) and affects the expression of 6/9 genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data.

claim: UME6, LYS14, and HMS1 mutants do not affect the expression of the core TFs involved in filament initiation.
source: UME6, LYS14, and HMS1 mutants do not affect the expression of the core TFs involved in filament initiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data.

claim: The hms1∆∆ and lys14∆∆ mutants have minimal overlap with the genes regulated by Rob1.
source: The hms1∆∆ and lys14∆∆ mutants have minimal overlap with the genes regulated by Rob1, while nearly half the genes regulated by Ume6 are shared with Rob1 (Figure 7B), although that represents less than 25% of the genes regulated by Rob1.
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Nearly half the genes regulated by Ume6 are shared with Rob1.
source: The hms1∆∆ and lys14∆∆ mutants have minimal overlap with the genes regulated by Rob1, while nearly half the genes regulated by Ume6 are shared with Rob1 (Figure 7B), although that represents less than 25% of the genes regulated by Rob1.
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In vivo, Ume6, Hms1, and Lys14 are required for the full expression of 32, 23, and 29 genes, respectively.
source: In vivo, Ume6, Hms1, and Lys14 are required for the full expression of 32, 23, and 29 genes, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data.

claim: Hms1 and Lys14 have 17 genes in common.
source: Hms1 and Lys14 have 17 genes in common (Figure 7C); Lys14 has only 5 genes which it uniquely regulates.
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Lys14 has only 5 genes which it uniquely regulates.
source: Hms1 and Lys14 have 17 genes in common (Figure 7C); Lys14 has only 5 genes which it uniquely regulates.
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis.

claim: Ume6 has the largest set of uniquely regulated genes (16 genes) among the three elongation-associated TFs.
source: Ume6 has the largest set of uniquely regulated genes (16 genes).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis.

claim: Ume6 shares more targets with hyphae initiation-associated TFs relative to Lys14 and Hms1.
source: Although Ume6, Lys14, and Hms1 all selectively affect elongation, Ume6 does seem to share more targets with hyphae initiation-associated TFs relative to Lys14 and Hms1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the overlap analysis of gene expression data.

claim: 9/23 genes regulated by at least two of the hyphal elongation TFs are cell wall or secreted proteins.
source: Specifically, 9/23 genes (ALS2, ALS9, CRH11, RBT1, SAP1, SAP10, SCW4, SCW11, SOG2; Supplementary file 5) regulated by at least two of hyphal elongation TFs are cell wall or secreted proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of transcriptional profiling data.

claim: Elongation-associated TFs regulate cell wall remodeling during the elongation phase of filamentation.
source: This correlation suggests that elongation-associated TFs regulate cell wall remodeling during the elongation phase of filamentation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that many genes regulated by elongation TFs encode cell wall proteins.

claim: Elongation-associated TFs regulate a distinct set of genes relative to TFs required for the initiation of filamentation.
source: Overall, our profiling of these mutants indicates that they regulate a distinct set of genes relative to TFs required for the initiation of filamentation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparison of transcriptional profiling data for initiation and elongation TFs.

claim: Repressors of C. albicans filamentation in vitro include Nrg1, Tup1, Ssn6, and Rfg1.
source: In vitro, repressors of C. albicans filamentation include Nrg1, Tup1, Ssn6, and Rfg1.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about repressors of filamentation.

claim: 16 TF deletion mutants were hyper-filamentous on at least one condition in vitro.
source: Although Homann et al. found that 16 TF deletion mutants were hyper-filamentous on at least one condition in vitro (Homann et al., 2009), our in vivo screen of the same deletion set found that the nrg1∆∆ and tup1∆∆ mutants were the only two with statistically significant increases in percentage filamentous cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The nrg1∆∆ and tup1∆∆ mutants were the only two with statistically significant increases in percentage filamentous cells in vivo.
source: Although Homann et al. found that 16 TF deletion mutants were hyper-filamentous on at least one condition in vitro (Homann et al., 2009), our in vivo screen of the same deletion set found that the nrg1∆∆ and tup1∆∆ mutants were the only two with statistically significant increases in percentage filamentous cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the genetic screen.

claim: Deletion mutants of NRG1 and TUP1 were the only two that formed longer filaments than the WT strain.
source: Similarly, deletion mutants of NRG1 and TUP1 were the only two that formed longer filaments than the WT strain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the genetic screen.

claim: The tup1∆∆ mutant forms nearly 100% filaments in vitro and in vivo.
source: The tup1∆∆ mutant forms nearly 100% filaments in vitro and in vivo while the efg1∆∆ mutant forms almost no filaments under either condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The efg1∆∆ mutant forms almost no filaments in vitro and in vivo.
source: The tup1∆∆ mutant forms nearly 100% filaments in vitro and in vivo while the efg1∆∆ mutant forms almost no filaments under either condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The tup1∆∆ efg1∆∆ double mutant forms approximately 20% filamentous cells in vitro and in vivo.
source: The tup1∆∆ efg1∆∆ double mutant forms approximately 20% filamentous cells in vitro and in vivo (Figure 8A), indicating the relief of Tup1 repression requires Efg1 for filamentation to proceed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Relief of Tup1 repression requires Efg1 for filamentation to proceed.
source: The tup1∆∆ efg1∆∆ double mutant forms approximately 20% filamentous cells in vitro and in vivo (Figure 8A), indicating the relief of Tup1 repression requires Efg1 for filamentation to proceed.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic interaction data.

claim: The nrg1∆∆ mutant forms predominantly hyphae in vitro.
source: In vitro, the nrg1∆∆ mutant forms predominantly hyphae while nrg1∆∆ double mutants with the three positive regulators formed very few hyphae with pseudohyphae as the dominant morphotype (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: nrg1∆∆ double mutants with the three positive regulators (brg1∆∆, efg1∆∆, rob1∆∆) formed very few hyphae with pseudohyphae as the dominant morphotype in vitro.
source: In vitro, the nrg1∆∆ mutant forms predominantly hyphae while nrg1∆∆ double mutants with the three positive regulators formed very few hyphae with pseudohyphae as the dominant morphotype (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: All three double mutants (brg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆, efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆, rob1∆∆ nrg1∆∆) formed similar numbers of filaments as wild type cells in vivo.
source: In vivo, all three double mutants formed similar numbers of filaments as wild type (WT) cells (Figure 8D, E) whereas the single mutants of BRG1, EFG1, and ROB1 are significantly deficient (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D and 8E.

claim: Deletion of NRG1 suppresses the in vivo filamentation defect of all three of the major TF regulators of in vivo filamentation (Brg1, Efg1, Rob1).
source: Thus, deletion of NRG1 suppresses the in vivo filamentation defect of all three of the major TF regulators of in vivo filamentation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic interaction data showing that nrg1∆∆ double mutants filament normally.

claim: The nrg1∆∆ mutants showed increased branching relative to WT cells in vivo.
source: We noticed that the nrg1∆∆ mutants showed increased branching relative to WT cells in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Increased branching of filaments is a characteristic of pseudohyphae.
source: Increased branching of filaments is a characteristic of pseudohyphae (Sudbery et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: WT cells branch very little in vivo, suggesting that hyphae are the predominant morphotype at the 24 hr time point.
source: In our experience, WT cells branch very little in vivo, suggesting that hyphae are the predominant morphotype at the time point that we are analyzing (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental observations shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Deletion of NRG1 increases the extent of branching to almost 50%.
source: Deletion of NRG1 increases the extent of branching to almost 50% (Figure 8F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The branching phenotype of nrg1∆∆ is preserved in the brg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ and rob1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutants.
source: The branching phenotype of nrg1∆∆ is preserved in the brg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ and rob1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutants, while the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant modest branching relative to nrg1∆∆.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant has modest branching relative to nrg1∆∆.
source: The branching phenotype of nrg1∆∆ is preserved in the brg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ and rob1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutants, while the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant modest branching relative to nrg1∆∆.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The filaments formed by the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant are more hyphae-like than the nrg1∆∆ mutant.
source: This indicates that the filaments formed by the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant are more hyphae-like than the nrg1∆∆ mutant.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the branching phenotype data.

claim: ACE2 is expressed at very high levels in the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ double mutant (FC 13.8 relative to WT; q value = 0.002).
source: A possible explanation for the reduced branching of the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant relative to the nrg1∆∆ single mutant is that the TF ACE2 is expressed at very high levels in the double mutant (FC 13.8 relative to WT; q value = 0.002, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data.

claim: Efg1 suppresses ACE2 expression in vitro and binds to the promoter of ACE2.
source: We have previously shown that Efg1 suppresses ACE2 expression in vitro and binds to the promoter of ACE2 (Saputo et al., 2014); ACE2 expression is also increased in the efg1∆∆ mutant in vivo (FC 6.1 relative to WT q value = 0.04, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: ACE2 expression is increased in the efg1∆∆ mutant in vivo (FC 6.1 relative to WT q value = 0.04).
source: We have previously shown that Efg1 suppresses ACE2 expression in vitro and binds to the promoter of ACE2 (Saputo et al., 2014); ACE2 expression is also increased in the efg1∆∆ mutant in vivo (FC 6.1 relative to WT q value = 0.04, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data.

claim: Ace2 suppresses lateral yeast formation during in vitro filamentation.
source: We have also demonstrated that Ace2 suppresses lateral yeast formation during in vitro filamentation (Wakade and Krysan, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The increased expression of ACE2 in the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant suggests that loss of Efg1 leads to increased ACE2 expression which in turn reduces lateral branching.
source: Thus, the increased expression of ACE2 in the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant suggests that loss of Efg1 leads to increased ACE2 expression which in turn reduces lateral branching.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the transcriptional profiling data and previous knowledge about Ace2 function.

claim: The expression of ALS3, ECE1, and HWP1 are all significantly reduced in the TF single mutants (efg1∆∆, brg1∆∆, rob1∆∆).
source: The expression of ALS3, ECE1, and HWP1 are all significantly reduced in the TF single mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data.

claim: In the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant, the expression of ALS3, ECE1, and HWP1 is restored to WT levels.
source: In the case of the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant, the expression of all three canonical hypha-associated genes is restored to WT levels; of the remaining genes, only SAP6 expression is reduced in the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data shown in Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only SAP6 expression is reduced in the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant among the hyphae-associated genes.
source: In the case of the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant, the expression of all three canonical hypha-associated genes is restored to WT levels; of the remaining genes, only SAP6 expression is reduced in the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Three separate groups have found that Efg1 directly binds the promoters of ALS3, ECE1, and HWP1.
source: This is a rather surprising result because three separate groups have found that Efg1 directly binds the promoters of these genes (Lassak et al., 2011; Witchley et al., 2021; Do et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Efg1 is not necessary for the expression of ALS3, ECE1, and HWP1 as well as other hypha-specific genes after relief of Nrg1 expression.
source: However, our data indicate that Efg1 is not necessary for the expression of ALS3, ECE1, and HWP1 as well as other hypha-specific genes after relief of Nrg1 expression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the transcriptional profiling data showing these genes are expressed in the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant.

claim: Rob1 and Brg1 play a consistent role in the expression of the hypha-associated genes in vivo and in vitro.
source: Rob1 and Brg1, on the other hand, play a consistent role in the expression of the hypha-associated genes in vivo and in vitro with Rob1 having a more important role for most of the genes that we analyzed (Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data shown in Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rob1 has a more important role than Brg1 for the expression of most hypha-associated genes.
source: Rob1 and Brg1, on the other hand, play a consistent role in the expression of the hypha-associated genes in vivo and in vitro with Rob1 having a more important role for most of the genes that we analyzed (Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data shown in Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Efg1 functions upstream of Nrg1 and may mediate the relief of Nrg1 repression rather than the direct induction of hypha-specific gene expression after relief of Nrg1 repression.
source: In terms of regulation of hypha-induced genes, our data suggest that Efg1 functions upstream of Nrg1 and may mediate the relief of Nrg1 repression rather than the direct induction of hypha-specific gene expression after relief of Nrg1 repression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic interaction and transcriptional profiling data.

claim: 49 genes have reduced expression in the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant relative to WT in vivo.
source: Although Efg1 does not appear to contribute directly to the expression of canonical hyphae-associated genes after relief of Nrg1 repression, 49 genes have reduced expression in the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant relative to WT in vivo as indicated by the Venn diagram in Figure 9B.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Of the 49 genes with reduced expression in the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant, the promoters of nearly 50% (22/49) have been shown to be bound by Efg1 in vitro.
source: Of these 49 genes, the promoters of nearly 50% (22/49) have been shown to be bound by Efg1 in vitro while only three have Nrg1 Responsive Elements (NRE, Murad et al., 2001) in their promoter regions (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of transcriptional profiling data with published ChIP data and promoter analysis.

claim: Only three of the 49 genes with reduced expression in the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant have Nrg1 Responsive Elements (NRE) in their promoter regions.
source: Of these 49 genes, the promoters of nearly 50% (22/49) have been shown to be bound by Efg1 in vitro while only three have Nrg1 Responsive Elements (NRE, Murad et al., 2001) in their promoter regions (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by promoter analysis using published NRE sequences.

claim: All Efg1 bound genes whose expression was restored to WT levels in the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant deletion contained NRE sequences in their promoter.
source: In contrast, all Efg1 bound genes whose expression was restored to WT levels in the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant deletion contained NRE sequences in their promoter (Figure 9B), suggesting that they are directly bound by Nrg1.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of transcriptional profiling data with promoter analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Efg1 bound genes whose expression was restored to WT levels in the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant are directly bound by Nrg1.
source: In contrast, all Efg1 bound genes whose expression was restored to WT levels in the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant deletion contained NRE sequences in their promoter (Figure 9B), suggesting that they are directly bound by Nrg1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the presence of NRE sequences in the promoters of these genes.

claim: Efg1 and Nrg1 appear to bind a common set of hypha-associated genes during filament initiation but Efg1 is not required for their expression.
source: From these data, Efg1 and Nrg1 appears to bind a common set of hypha-associated genes during filament initiation but Efg1 is not required for their expression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the transcriptional profiling and promoter analysis data.

claim: Rob1 and Brg1 along with additional TFs contribute to the expression of Nrg1-repressed, hypha-associated genes.
source: Most likely, Rob1 and Brg1 along with additional TFs contribute to the expression of Nrg1-repressed, hypha-associated genes.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that these genes are expressed in the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant.

claim: After relief of Nrg1 repression, Efg1 binds to the promoters and regulates the expression of a second set of genes that are not repressed by Nrg1.
source: After relief of Nrg1 repression, Efg1 binds to the promoters and regulates the expression of a second set of genes that are not repressed by Nrg1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the analysis of genes that remain downregulated in the efg1∆∆ nrg1∆∆ mutant.

claim: Efg1 indirectly regulates hyphae-specific genes, possibly by mediating the displacement of Nrg1 from their promoters.
source: Since canonical hyphae-specific genes are in the first class of Efg1 targets, our data are consistent with the surprising result that Efg1 indirectly regulates hyphae-specific genes, possibly by mediating the displacement of Nrg1 from their promoters.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism by which Efg1 regulates hyphae-specific genes based on the genetic interaction and transcriptional profiling data.
